lessons.title: Knowing the problem animals
lessons.html:
What is a problem animal?

A problem animal is a wild or stray animal that kills our livestock, eats our crops or damages the farm. On South African farms the common problem animals are:

  • Black-backed jackal – kills lambs, kids and sometimes sheep.
  • Caracal (rooikat) – kills sheep, goats and lambs.
  • Stray and feral dogs – can kill many sheep in one night.
  • Baboons and monkeys – eat fruit, maize and vegetables, and can kill lambs.
  • Bushpigs and porcupines – dig up and eat crops like maize, potatoes and pumpkins.
  • Rats and mice – eat and dirty stored feed and spread disease.

Find out what did it

When you find a dead animal, do not move it at once. Look carefully and tell your supervisor.

  1. Look for bite marks on the throat, neck or back.
  2. Look for tracks in the sand or mud around it.
  3. Look for dung (scat) nearby.
  4. Check if there is blood or bruising at the bite. Bleeding means the animal was alive when it was bitten.
  5. Count how many animals are dead or hurt, and where.

Sometimes an animal died of sickness or cold, and a jackal ate it later. Then the jackal did not kill it. Your supervisor needs the right facts to choose the right action.

Write it down

Write the date, the camp, the kind of animal killed and what you saw. These records help the farm see where and when losses happen.

lessons.title: Protecting livestock and crops
lessons.html:
Prevent losses first

It is better to stop a problem animal from getting to the stock than to kill it afterwards. Here are ways the farm can protect animals and crops.

For sheep and goats

  • Bring sheep and goats into the kraal at night.
  • Keep ewes that are lambing in camps close to the house.
  • Use guard animals such as Anatolian dogs, donkeys or alpacas that live with the flock.
  • Check the flock every day; a herder with the flock helps a lot.
  • Fit lamb collars if the farm uses them.
  • Remove dead animals quickly so they do not attract jackals.

Fences

  • Walk the fences often. Look for holes under the fence where jackals dig through.
  • Fix holes at once and tell your supervisor about big damage.
  • Check that electric fence wires are working and not touching grass or bushes.

For crops and stores

  • Keep fences around lands and orchards in good repair.
  • Pick up fallen fruit and do not leave food or rubbish lying around, because it attracts baboons and monkeys.
  • Keep feed stores closed and clean, and feed in bins with lids, to keep rats out.

Watch and report

Tell your supervisor if you see tracks, hear jackals calling, or see baboons near the lands. Early warning gives the farm time to act.

lessons.title: Working safely and within the law
lessons.html:
Only approved methods

Wild animals are protected by law. Some, like leopards and brown hyenas, may not be killed at all without a permit. The farm manager must check with the nature conservation office what methods are allowed. You must only use the methods your supervisor tells you, and only after you are trained.

Never do these things

  • Never put out poison on your own. Poison kills dogs, birds, other wild animals and can kill people, especially children.
  • Never set traps that are not allowed on the farm.
  • Never use a firearm unless you have a licence and you are trained, as the Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000 requires.
  • Never make an animal suffer. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 says animals must not be treated cruelly.

Traps

If the farm uses cage traps, check them every day, early in the morning. A trapped animal must not be left to suffer. Do not go close to a trapped jackal, caracal, baboon or bushpig. They bite and scratch badly. Call your supervisor or the trained person.

Stay safe

  • Wear gloves when you touch dead animals; they can carry disease.
  • Wash your hands after handling carcasses or traps.
  • Keep away from baboons; do not look them in the eyes or try to chase a big troop alone.
  • If you are bitten or scratched, wash the wound well with soap and water and get medical help, because of the risk of rabies.

Key points

  • Know the common problem animals on your farm.
  • Look for bite marks, tracks and dung, and report what you find.
  • Prevent losses with kraals, guard animals, herders and good fences.
  • Only use methods your supervisor allows; never use poison on your own.
  • Stay away from trapped wild animals and get medical help for bites.
